source.title_on_document: Generative AI adoption in human creative tasks: Experimental evidence

supplement.where: Appendix E (p. 21): 'Supplementary material related to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107414.'
supplement.holds: Pre-registration and deviations (Section 1); rationale for the evaluation method (Sections 1.2-1.3); robustness Tables S1-S7 (standardized grades, by theme, individual/team-level analysis in Table S4, idea-evaluator level in Table S5, evaluator subsets); mediation Tables S9-S10; Figure S1 (effects by DAT quartile); instructions, training materials, screenshots and example ideas/images (Section 3, 3.5).

paper_design_summary: In a pre-registered lab experiment at Nankai University (first wave, 2023), 246 students were randomly assigned to work alone (HI, control), alone with access to ChatGPT 3.5 (HAT), or in anonymous two-person teams (HHT) on two 12-minute tasks in which they wrote an idea (under 100 Chinese characters) for a creative picture. A second wave (2024) added 56 students in a Training treatment (HAT plus three prior ChatGPT training sessions), which the authors do not treat as causally identified. Each idea was turned into an image with DALL-E 3 and rated 1-10 by 30 student evaluators per task, on text plus image (primary) and on text only; ten ChatGPT-only ideas per theme were rated alongside.

studies.label: Wave 1 lab experiment: Control (HI) vs ChatGPT access (HAT) vs human-human team (HHT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Treatment for tasks 2-3: work alone (HI), work alone with ChatGPT 3.5 access (HAT), or work in a randomly matched anonymous pair (HHT). Task 1 was done alone by everyone before treatment.
assignment.quote: In the first wave, 246 participants were recruited and randomly assigned to one of three between-subject treatments.
assignment.locator: p. 2, Section 1; p. 4, Section 2.1 and Table 1; p. 19, Table D.2 (No. sessions: HI 2, HAT 2, HHT 5)

arms.name: HAT (Human-AI Team)
arms.description: Tasks 2-3 done individually with access to ChatGPT 3.5 via poe.com

arms.name: HHT (Human-Human Team)
arms.description: Tasks 2-3 done in anonymous pairs, rematched for each task (61 teams), chatting by text and submitting one joint idea

participants.exclusions: One HAT participant was excluded from grade analyses because all ChatGPT interaction data were missing (p. 17, Appendix B.2). Image-text grades also have missing outputs: 46 of 784 prompts failed image generation and some evaluator grades are missing (p. 17, B.2), so Table 2 image-text submissions are HI 116 and HAT 116 versus text-only 126 and 120.
participants.who: University students recruited to the Laboratory for Economic Behavior and Policy Simulation, Nankai University; mean age about 21.4; tasks done in Chinese
participants.quote: participants in the HI treatment (N = 63) continued to work individually, while participants in the HAT treatment (N = 61) were able to interact with ChatGPT 3.5 ... participants in the HHT treatment (N = 122) collaborated in anonymous pairs
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 6, Section 2.3; p. 17, Appendix B.2; p. 19, Table D.2

ai_tool.how_used: HAT participants could freely prompt ChatGPT while writing their idea in tasks 2 and 3 (on average 15 prompts over the two tasks); all arms had a 12-minute free ChatGPT familiarization period before task 1.

task.description: Write an idea for a creative picture on a given theme ('Surprisingly, he/she/it is here!' and '... is learning this new skill!'), under 100 Chinese characters; ideas were rendered as images with DALL-E 3 and rated. Incentivized by linear pay on grades plus a tournament bonus.
task.duration: 12 minutes per task (soft limit); two treated tasks (tasks 2 and 3), theme order counterbalanced

outcomes.name: Creativity grade, image-text evaluation
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean of 30 student research assistants' 1-10 creativity ratings (one decimal) of each idea shown with its DALL-E 3 image; evaluators blind to treatment; Cronbach's alpha 0.89 (here) and 0.86 (skill). Robustness in Supplement: standardized grades (S1), by theme (S2-S3), individual/team level (S4), idea-evaluator level (S5), evaluator subsets (S6-S7).

outcomes.name: Inequality of creative performance (coefficient of variation of grades; Gini of implied payments)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Dispersion of image-text grades across participants within each treatment and theme: CV = SD/mean of grades; Gini coefficient of payments under a linear payment rule without a fixed payment. This is dispersion of quality, not similarity of content.

contrasts.reported: CV: Here 0.072 (Control) vs 0.062 (HAT); Skill 0.155 vs 0.137. Gini: Here 0.040 vs 0.035; Skill 0.089 vs 0.077. No tests reported.

outcomes.name: Post-treatment Divergent Association Task (DAT) score and modified-DAT score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT: 10 nouns as different as possible, translated to English, mean pairwise GloVe semantic distance x 100. Modified DAT: one noun as dissimilar as possible from each of six given words, mean GloVe distance. Administered after Questionnaire II, following task 3; regression of post score on treatment dummies controlling for pre score and unbalanced covariates. Table 1 lists ChatGPT access only for tasks 2-3; the paper does not state explicitly that ChatGPT was unavailable during the second DAT.
outcomes.delay: Same session, after tasks 2-3 and Questionnaire II

contrasts.reported: 'experiencing ChatGPT access and experiencing teamwork both lead to an increase of 0.19 SDs in the modified-DAT score; their effect on the DAT score are not statistically significant.' Coefficients with 95% CIs plotted in Fig. 4b; no table.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Zhu and Zou (2023), the authors' earlier working paper, which analyzed the first-wave participants with two-evaluator ratings (an earlier version of this study, not a separate sample). Holzner et al. (2025) meta-analysis includes the study.
sample_overlap.quote: we followed the prevailing approach in the literature by using average ratings from two evaluators as a measure of the creative performance, as reported in our earlier working paper (Zhu and Zou, 2023).

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned 246 students (p. 2) to ChatGPT access (HAT, 61) vs working alone (HI, 63) vs human pairs (HHT, 122); 245 people analyzed for grades (HAT+HI = 123), and the outcome is a 30-rater creativity grade of the written idea. Caveat: Table D.2 shows each arm ran in separate sessions (HI 2, HAT 2), so treatment may have varied by session; SEs are clustered by session. The Training arm (S2) is a later, non-random wave and is not core.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT access raised image-text creativity grades by 0.24 points (0.32 SD, p < .01; control mean 5.93) relative to working alone (p. 8, Table 3 col 2), while the text-only effect was smaller and not significant with controls (0.090, SE 0.094; Table 3 col 5).
open_questions: Assignment unit: the paper says participants were randomly assigned, but Table D.2 (p. 19) lists separate sessions per arm (HI 2, HAT 2, HHT 5, Training 2). Was treatment randomized by session? With 2 clusters per arm, session-clustered SEs are fragile.

Appendix B.2 (p. 17) says all 302 subjects were 'randomly distributed across four groups', and the abstract says 302 were assigned with a random subset given ChatGPT, but Sections 1 and 2.1 say the 56 Training participants were recruited in a later wave and are not causally comparable.
Whether ChatGPT was unavailable during the post-treatment DAT (S1-O4) is implied by Table 1 but not stated; the DAT effects are only in Fig. 4b and text, with no n.
Participant-level analysis (Table S4) and standardized grades (Table S1) are in the online supplement, not in this PDF.
notes: Main regressions (Table 3) are random-effects models at the individual/team-idea level with session-clustered SEs (11 sessions in total). Standardized effects in the text divide the coefficient by the SD of the outcome variable (p. 18, Appendix C). Heterogeneity by baseline DAT (Table 4, Fig. 2: inverted-U) and mediation analyses (Tables 7-8: word overlap, keyword origin, image-text minus text-only) are not listed as separate outcomes. Self-reported outcomes (satisfaction, self-efficacy, self-rated skills, AI opinions, WTP; Fig. 4, Table 6) do not qualify and are omitted. Task 4 manner was set by a BDM mechanism, and its grades are not reported. No diversity (across-people similarity) outcome is reported. Data 'will be made available on request' (p. 15).
